charts.title: Cost of owning vs renting, US typical home
charts.takeaway: Owning costs 1.72x renting with a 2% risk premium and 1.32x without one, up from 1.06x and 0.74x on average in 2015–19.
charts.source: Ledger model on FHFA, Census ACS, BLS, Freddie Mac, Treasury, FEMA

charts.title: Cost of owning vs renting, 50 largest metros
charts.takeaway: Among the 50 largest metros, owning costs the most relative to renting in San Jose (3.24x with a 2% risk premium); owning costs more than renting in 50 of 50 even without the premium.
charts.source: Ledger model on FHFA, Census ACS, BLS, Freddie Mac, Treasury FIO, FEMA

charts.title: US housing shortfall (+) or surplus (−) since 2010
charts.takeaway: The US built about 2.3 million fewer homes than household growth required from 2010 to 2024 (other assumptions give anything from a 2.6M surplus to a shortfall of 8.1M); the gap narrowed in 2025.
charts.source: Ledger model on Census ACS, HVS and New Residential Construction

charts.title: New homes permitted per month, city permit feeds
charts.takeaway: In the 12 months to Aug 2026, the 4 validated city feeds permitted 33,511 new homes, 67% more than a year earlier; Los Angeles permitted the most.
charts.source: City open-data permit feeds (Seattle, Austin, San Francisco, Los Angeles)

notes: Ranges are 10th–90th percentiles of 2,000 draws: US owning vs renting 1.44–1.79x (2% risk premium) and 1.04–1.39x (none).
The risk premium is an extra 2%-of-value yearly charge for bearing price risk, not a cash cost; both versions are shown because the answer depends on it.

Rents are Census median gross rents (all renters, utilities included) moved forward with the BLS rent index, so ratio levels differ from listing-rent measures; trends and rankings are the robust part.
Housing shortfall plausible range for 2010–24: -2.6M to +8.1M units (negative = surplus), depending on demolition rate (0–0.25%/yr) and normal vacancy (±2 points).
Price to income is shown on the ACS 2024 survey basis (4.42x) to match the state map; moved forward with FHFA prices and wage growth it is about 4.28x in 2026-07.
New York City permits are collected but left out: the feed does not match Census permit counts (annual correlation 0.44, monthly 0.17).
Each metro's figure assumes no tax deduction, while the draws allow up to 15%, so it can sit at or above the top of its range; the rank band also varies expected appreciation by metro.
Recent months of city permit data are incomplete and are revised as cities update their portals.
